subject: biology
title: Biology MYP 5 eAssessment Structure Mock B (8 tasks, 74 marks)

questions.content:
[[Q 1 | A 6]]
The human circulatory system carries blood around the body.
(a) State the name of the type of blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. (1 mark)
(b) Veins contain valves. State the function of these valves. (1 mark)
(c) Explain how the structure of a capillary makes it suited to exchanging substances with body cells. (2 marks)
(d) The wall of the left ventricle is much thicker than the wall of the right ventricle. Explain why. (2 marks)

Total for Question 1: 6 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Artery [1]. (b) To stop the backflow of blood (keep blood flowing towards the heart) [1]. (c) The wall is only one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance [1]; capillaries are very narrow and form a large network, giving a large surface area and slow flow so there is time for exchange [1]. (d) The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body, which needs a high pressure [1]; the right ventricle only pumps blood to the nearby lungs, which needs a lower pressure, so a thinner muscle wall is enough [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 2 | A 7]]
Cells release energy from glucose by respiration.
(a) Write the balanced chemical equation for aerobic respiration. (2 marks)
(b) State the name of the part of the cell where most aerobic respiration takes place. (1 mark)
(c) During a sprint, muscle cells also respire without oxygen. State the product of this process in muscle cells. (1 mark)
(d) Explain why a person keeps breathing heavily for several minutes after a sprint has finished. (2 marks)
(e) State one product of anaerobic respiration in yeast that is used to make bread rise. (1 mark)

Total for Question 2: 7 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O: correct reactants and products [1]; correctly balanced [1] (award 1 for the correct word equation). (b) Mitochondria (mitochondrion) [1]. (c) Lactic acid [1]. (d) The extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid that built up (the oxygen debt) [1]; the lactic acid is converted to carbon dioxide and water, or removed by the liver, and the muscles are restored to resting state [1]. (e) Carbon dioxide [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 3 | A 7]]
Cystic fibrosis is an inherited condition caused by a recessive allele, f. The dominant allele is F. Two parents who do not have cystic fibrosis each carry one copy of the recessive allele.
(a) State the genotype of each parent. (1 mark)
(b) Complete a Punnett square for the cross and determine the probability that their child has cystic fibrosis. (2 marks)
(c) Define the term allele. (1 mark)
(d) Describe the structure of a DNA molecule. (2 marks)
(e) State what a gene codes for. (1 mark)

Total for Question 3: 7 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Ff (both parents) [1]. (b) Gametes F and f from each parent; offspring FF, Ff, Ff, ff correctly shown [1]; probability = 1 in 4 (0.25 or 25%) [1]. (c) A different version of a gene [1]. (d) Two strands wound into a double helix [1]; held together by pairs of bases, A with T and C with G (accept: made of nucleotides with a sugar-phosphate backbone) [1]. (e) A protein (the order of amino acids in a protein) [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 4 | A 8]]
On a hot day a runner's body temperature starts to rise above its normal value.
(a) State the name of the part of the brain that monitors body temperature. (1 mark)
(b) Describe two ways in which the skin responds to a rise in body temperature. (4 marks)
(c) State the normal core body temperature of a healthy person. (1 mark)
(d) Explain how this response is an example of negative feedback. (2 marks)

Total for Question 4: 8 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Hypothalamus [1]. (b) Any two responses, each with a description and a reason (2 marks each): sweat glands release more sweat [1]; the evaporation of sweat takes heat from the skin and cools the body [1]. Blood vessels near the skin surface widen (vasodilation) [1]; more blood flows near the surface so more heat is lost by radiation to the surroundings [1]. (Accept hairs lying flat as a third response.) (c) About 37 degrees Celsius [1]. (d) A change away from the set point (a rise in temperature) is detected [1]; the response reverses the change and returns the temperature towards the set point [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 5 | B 10]]
A student wants to investigate how temperature affects the rate of anaerobic respiration in yeast. The student mixes dried yeast with sugar solution in a boiling tube. A delivery tube leads from the boiling tube into limewater in a second tube. The student can heat the boiling tube in a water bath.
(a) State a research question that this investigation could answer. (2 marks)
(b) Formulate a testable hypothesis, using scientific reasoning. (2 marks)
(c) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable. (2 marks)
(d) Outline a method that would allow the student to measure the rate of respiration at different temperatures. (3 marks)
(e) Outline one safety precaution for this investigation. (1 mark)

Total for Question 5: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) A question that links both variables, for example: How does the temperature of the yeast and sugar mixture affect the rate of carbon dioxide production? [2] (1 mark if both variables are named but not linked). (b) A prediction, for example: as the temperature increases up to about 40 degrees Celsius the rate will increase, then fall at higher temperatures [1]; reasoning using enzymes: respiration is controlled by enzymes, which work faster as particles gain energy but denature at high temperature [1]. (c) Independent: temperature of the mixture [1]; dependent: rate of carbon dioxide production, for example bubbles per minute or time for limewater to turn cloudy [1]. (d) Set up water baths at several temperatures, for example 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 degrees Celsius, and allow the mixture to reach each temperature [1]; at each temperature count the bubbles in the limewater tube (or measure the volume of gas in a syringe) over the same time, for example 5 minutes [1]; keep the volume and concentration of yeast and sugar, and the yeast mass, the same, and repeat the experiment to calculate a mean [1]. (e) Any one from: take care with hot water and hot glassware; wear eye protection; do not drink or taste the limewater and wash hands afterwards [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 6 | C 10]]
A student investigates transpiration using a potometer. The capillary tube of the potometer has an internal radius of 0.50 mm. The student records how far an air bubble moves along the tube in 10 minutes for the same leafy shoot in four conditions.
Condition: still air, moving air (fan), humid air, bright light
Distance moved by the bubble in 10 minutes in mm: 42, 78, 18, 60
The volume of water taken in is given by volume = pi x r squared x distance, where r is the radius of the tube.
(a) Show that the volume of water taken up in still air in 10 minutes is about 33 cubic millimetres. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the rate of water uptake in moving air, in cubic millimetres per minute. Give your answer to 2 significant figures. (3 marks)
(c) Calculate the percentage increase in the distance moved by the bubble in moving air compared with still air. (2 marks)
(d) Explain why the shoot takes up water more slowly in humid air. (2 marks)
(e) Evaluate one limitation of using a potometer to measure the rate of transpiration. (1 mark)

Total for Question 6: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Volume = pi x 0.50 squared x 42 [1] = 32.99 cubic millimetres, so about 33 [1]. (b) Volume = pi x 0.50 squared x 78 = 61.26 cubic millimetres [1]; divide by 10 minutes [1]; rate = 6.1 cubic millimetres per minute [1] (error carried forward is allowed). (c) (78 - 42) / 42 x 100 [1] = 86% (85.7%) [1]. (d) In humid air there is already a lot of water vapour in the air, so the concentration gradient of water vapour between the leaf and the air is smaller [1]; less water vapour diffuses out through the stomata, so transpiration and uptake of water are slower [1]. (e) A potometer measures water taken up, not water lost, and some water is used for photosynthesis or stays in the plant (accept: cutting the shoot and leaks of air affect the results; only one shoot was used) [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 7 | D 10]]
Read the passage.
Hospital scientists in a fictional country are using three new technologies. A bioprinter lays down layers of a gel mixed with a patient's own cells to build patches of skin for burn victims. The team hopes to print whole kidneys in the future. In a second project, the genomes of tumour cells are mapped so that doctors can choose the drug most likely to work. The data are stored on a company's computers. In a third, a company offers to clone a customer's pet dog for a high fee, using a cell from the dog's skin. Only a few of the cloned embryos develop into healthy animals.
(a) Define the term clone. (1 mark)
(b) Outline one benefit of mapping the genome of a patient's tumour. (1 mark)
(c) Explain why printing skin from the patient's own cells reduces the risk of rejection. (2 marks)
(d) Discuss one ethical factor related to cloning pets and one social factor related to storing genome data. (4 marks)
(e) Suggest one way in which the use of these technologies could be regulated, and justify your suggestion. (2 marks)

Total for Question 7: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) A genetically identical copy of an organism (or cell) [1]. (b) Doctors can choose a drug or treatment suited to the genetic changes in the tumour, so treatment is more effective (accept: faster diagnosis, fewer side effects) [1]. (c) The immune system recognises foreign cells by their antigens [1]; cells from the patient have the same antigens as the rest of the body, so the immune system does not attack the new tissue [1]. (d) Ethical (2 marks): most cloned embryos do not develop into healthy animals, causing suffering or waste of life [1]; developed, for example, the animal suffering is hard to justify for a pet, and the clone will not be identical in personality or experience [1]. Social (2 marks): genome data are private and could be used by insurers or employers to discriminate against people [1]; developed, for example, patients must give informed consent and be told who can access their data [1]. (e) A sensible suggestion, for example an independent ethics committee must approve each project, or laws limit who can see genome data [1]; with justification, for example this protects patients' rights and prevents misuse while still allowing medical benefit [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 8 | A 8 | C 4 | D 4]]
Read the passage and study the data.
Staphylococcus bacteria cause infections in hospital patients. Doctors use antibiotics to treat them. A hospital records the percentage of Staphylococcus samples that are resistant to a common antibiotic, and the number of prescriptions of this antibiotic for each 1000 patients.
Year: 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022
Samples resistant to the antibiotic (%): 4, 9, 19, 37
Prescriptions for each 1000 patients: 310, 420, 560, 700
(a) Explain how natural selection led to an increase in the percentage of resistant bacteria. (4 marks)
(b) Calculate how many times greater the percentage of resistant samples was in 2022 than in 2016. Give your answer to 2 significant figures. (2 marks)
(c) Describe the relationship between prescriptions and resistance and state why the data alone cannot prove that prescriptions cause resistance. (2 marks)
(d) Explain why a patient should finish a whole course of antibiotics, and why antibiotics are not used to treat viral infections. (4 marks)
(e) Evaluate two actions that hospitals could take to reduce antibiotic resistance, stating one advantage or drawback of each. (4 marks)

Total for Question 8: 16 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Variation exists in the bacteria because of random mutations, and a few bacteria are resistant [1]; the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria, so the resistant ones survive (selection pressure) [1]; the survivors reproduce and pass on the resistance allele to their offspring [1]; over many generations the proportion of resistant bacteria increases [1]. (b) 37 / 4 [1] = 9.25, so about 9.3 times (accept 9.2) [1]. (c) As prescriptions increase, the percentage of resistant samples also increases (positive correlation) [1]; correlation does not prove cause, because other factors may have changed, such as the number of patients with infections or hygiene (accept: more patients carrying resistant bacteria) [1]. (d) Finishing the course kills all the bacteria, including those that are less sensitive [1]; stopping early leaves survivors that can multiply, and these may be resistant [1]. Viruses are not living cells, and antibiotics work by damaging bacterial structures such as cell walls [1]; viruses live inside host cells and are not affected, so the antibiotic would not work and would only increase resistance [1]. (e) Any two actions each with an evaluation (2 marks each), for example: restrict prescriptions to confirmed bacterial infections [1], which slows the spread of resistance, but some patients might be under-treated [1]; improve hygiene such as hand washing and isolating infected patients [1], which reduces the spread of resistant bacteria without using drugs, but needs staff time and training [1]. (Accept: use a different antibiotic or two together, research into new antibiotics, vaccination.)
